cases.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: text with no full-width characters is returned unchanged
cases.expected_note: Microsoft's page publishes this example verbatim: '=ASC("EXCEL") equals "EXCEL"'. The documentation adds "If text does not contain any full-width letters, text is not changed"

cases.description: Full-width (double-byte) Latin letters converted to half-width
cases.expected_note: The page's second example is the same word in full-width characters, but it is rendered as inline images so the literal argument cannot be copied from the page; this case reconstructs it from the documented rule that the function "changes full-width (double-byte) characters to half-width (single-byte) characters". The argument is U+FF25 U+FF38 U+FF23 U+FF25 U+FF2C (FULLWIDTH LATIN CAPITAL E X C E L), whose documented half-width forms are the ASCII letters EXCEL

cases.description: Full-width letter, full-width digits and an ideographic space
cases.expected_note: Derived from the same documented full-width-to-half-width rule: U+FF21 -> A, U+FF11/FF12/FF13 -> 1/2/3, and U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE -> U+0020 half-width space, giving the five-character string "A123 " (trailing half-width space)

cases.description: The conversion is character-for-character, so the length is unchanged
cases.expected_note: Excel documents ASC as changing full-width characters to half-width characters, a one-for-one character mapping rather than an encoding change, so a five-character input yields a five-character result. This case separates a genuine width conversion from a byte-level reinterpretation
